title: The workflow map that made a complex operating system discussable
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

Contractor engagement, system access, invoicing and reconciliation looked like separate administrative tasks. In practice, they formed one lifecycle crossing operations, finance, QuickBooks, Excel, cloud storage, email and electronic signing.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| One lifecycle spread across several teams and tools | A visual end-to-end process model with explicit handovers, controls and exception paths | The team could discuss the same workflow before deciding what to standardise or automate |

## The real constraint

The hard part was not drawing boxes. It was exposing the dependencies that sat between them: a contractor could be engaged but not configured in the time system; an invoice workbook could exist but still contain the wrong details; a submitted invoice could be changed after review; a discrepancy could be found without a defined route back to the worker.

Without an end-to-end view, each team could optimise its own step while the handovers remained fragile.

## What Heutrix delivered

The process board connected four detailed views:

1. contractor engagement and agreement signing;
2. QuickBooks onboarding and access confirmation;
3. invoice-template setup and verification; and
4. the recurring pay-cycle workflow for workers, accounts and administrators.

The map named the systems involved, the information required at each transition, the verification checks, the manual decisions and the points where reminders or status automation were useful. It also separated the normal route from discrepancy handling and post-payment locking.

## The operating result

The map created a common operating model. It made clear that automation should support an agreed sequence, not compensate for an undefined one. It also gave later workbook, reminder and reporting work a stable design reference: each build could be traced to a specific handover or control in the lifecycle.

This was the first proof point: a complicated cross-system process became concrete enough to review, challenge and improve.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 4 connected lifecycle stages and more than 10 handoffs, checks or decision points brought into one shared model.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 15–30 minutes less cross-team clarification each time an onboarding or invoice exception moved between roles.

The efficiency range is an estimate based on the delivered workflow structure and the coordination steps made explicit.

## Evidence and limits

The source process board was reviewed directly in view-only mode. It contains the detailed lifecycle and named control points described above, and separate execution evidence is present for relevant automation components. The indicative efficiency range is not an audited productivity result, and this case makes no financial or compliance claim.

## Related Heutrix offering

This delivery reflects the core work of [Heutrix Diagnostics ](/services#heutrix-diagnostics): defining a workflow boundary, mapping the current state, exposing failure points and creating a decision-ready future state before implementation. The organisation retained responsibility for employment, screening, privacy, financial and regulatory decisions.
metric: Approximately 15–30 minutes less cross-team clarification each time an onboarding or invoice exception moved between roles.

title: A signed agreement became a controlled handover, not the end of an email thread
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

Bringing an independent support worker into the organisation required more than sending a contract. Details had to be checked, rates agreed, an agreement produced, signature fields assigned correctly and the final organisation signature applied in the right order.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Contract activity depended on individual memory and careful email handling | A sequenced engagement-and-signing workflow with verification before sending | Each handover had a visible purpose and a final check before the agreement moved forward |

## The real constraint

Electronic signing did not remove process risk on its own. The workflow still had to answer:

- which prerequisite information had been checked;
- which details belonged in the agreement;
- who should receive which signature fields;
- what signing order applied; and
- who performed the final verification.

The risk sat in the handoffs between qualification checks, agreement preparation and the signing platform.

## What Heutrix delivered

The mapped workflow began with initial engagement, qualification and detail checks. It then moved through rate negotiation, agreement generation and export to the electronic-signing tool.

The process specified separate contractor, witness and organisation recipients; the fields assigned to each; a signing order; a message for signatories; and a pre-send verification covering fields, recipients and contact details. The organisation signed only after the other required signatures were complete.

That sequence converted a tacit administrative routine into a repeatable operating path.

## The operating result

The team gained a clear definition of “ready to send” and “ready for final signature”. Work could be handed between people without relying on the original preparer to explain every step. The signing tool remained only one component; the workflow supplied the controls around it.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** Approximately 5 controlled checkpoints spanning prerequisites, agreement details, recipients, signing order and final verification.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 10–20 minutes less preparation and follow-up effort per agreement moving through the standard path.

The efficiency range is an estimate based on the repeatable checks and handoffs built into the delivered process. Client feedback supports that the sequenced handover operated as intended.

## Evidence and limits

The detailed engagement-and-contract process was reviewed on the source board, and client feedback supports the practical operation of the sequenced handover. This case does not claim that a particular screening, contracting or employment requirement was satisfied, and it is not legal or regulatory advice.

## Related Heutrix offering

This was delivered as a part of [Heutrix Workflow Transformation ](/services#heutrix-workflow-transformation): one bounded workflow with defined roles, handovers, agreed-tool configuration, verification points and an operating guide. The organisation and its qualified advisers remained accountable for the substantive contracting and employment requirements.
metric: Approximately 10–20 minutes less preparation and follow-up effort per agreement moving through the standard path.

title: QuickBooks onboarding gained a finish line: access accepted and configured
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

Creating a user in a time-tracking system is easy to mark as complete. The worker may still be unable to use it, assigned to the wrong group or missing the invoice setup that depends on their new identity.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| “User created” was treated as finished | A sequenced QuickBooks onboarding path ending in accepted access, correct grouping and verified invoice setup | The handover ended at usable configuration rather than an invitation email |

## The real constraint

The workflow crossed several small but dependent actions: capture contact details, create the account, send the invitation, allocate the appropriate groups, confirm acceptance and carry the worker identifier into the invoicing workbook.

If any step was assumed rather than checked, the failure appeared later—often when a worker needed to record time or submit an invoice.

## What Heutrix delivered

The onboarding process made each transition explicit:

1. capture the minimum worker details required for setup;
2. create the QuickBooks Time user;
3. send the invitation;
4. allocate the approved user groups;
5. verify that the invitation was accepted and onboarding completed; and
6. configure the corresponding invoice tabs, numbers and worker details.

The final checks covered invoice number, invoice date, pay cycle, payee information, business details and bank-deposit information. The workflow also required a check that no unintended pre-populated data remained before the template was protected and released.

## The operating result

The definition of done moved beyond “invite sent”. Administration could follow a consistent sequence from new starter to usable system access and correctly configured invoicing material. The process exposed unfinished setup before it reached a live pay cycle.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 6 defined steps from worker-detail capture through accepted system access and invoice configuration.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 1–4 hours less onboarding and corrective administration per worker.

The efficiency range is supported by client feedback and reflects the setup, follow-up and corrective work consolidated into the delivered onboarding path.

## Evidence and limits

The source board contains the complete QuickBooks onboarding and verification path. Supporting workbook artefacts show the linked invoice-tab and invoice-number structure, while client feedback supports the approximate 1–4-hour reduction in onboarding effort per worker. The range is not an audited time study. This case does not claim uninterrupted access, payroll accuracy or compliance with any employment or screening requirement.

title: Each contractor received a ready-to-use invoice workspace—not a blank spreadsheet
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

A generic invoice template shifted too much setup work to the pay cycle. Every new contractor created another chance to use the wrong file, number an invoice inconsistently or leave required details incomplete.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| A reusable template still required interpretation at each cycle | A configured workbook and cloud folder for each contractor, prepared and checked before use | Workers started from a controlled invoice workspace with the stable details already organised |

## The real constraint

The problem was not Excel itself. It was the absence of a repeatable setup process around the workbook: assign the worker identity, allocate an invoice range, create the folder, populate stable details, name the pay-cycle tabs and verify the release copy.

When those decisions happened informally, mistakes were discovered during reconciliation rather than during setup.

## What Heutrix delivered

The solution combined a master workbook with a defined configuration workflow:

- allocate a worker identifier and invoice-number range;
- create the worker’s timesheet and invoice folder;
- copy and rename the master template using a consistent convention;
- populate approved stable details in the sample sheet;
- prepare individual pay-cycle tabs for the financial year;
- verify invoice number, invoice date, pay cycle, payee details, business details and payment information;
- check that no unintended pre-populated data remained; and
- protect the workbook before uploading the release version.

The workbook itself included an invoice overview, sample invoice sheet, pay-cycle sheets and named fields for the contractor, pay cycle, invoice totals and reimbursement components.

## The operating result

Setup became a controlled onboarding deliverable rather than a task deferred to the first invoice. Each worker received a specific file in a known location, while accounts gained a consistent structure across the contractor group.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 8 repeatable setup and release checks applied to each contractor invoice workspace.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 1–2 hours less setup and first-cycle rework per new contractor.

The efficiency range is supported by client feedback and reflects the configuration, verification and rework steps consolidated by the delivered workflow.

## Evidence and limits

The process map and two master workbook versions support the configuration steps and workbook structure described here. Client feedback supports savings of up to approximately 2 hours per contractor. The range is not an audited cycle-time study, and this case makes no claim about financial accuracy or payment outcomes.

title: Formula-driven invoices protected the numbers that should not be free-typed
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

An invoice workbook needs two things that pull in opposite directions: workers must be able to enter legitimate shift information, while calculation and reference fields need protection from accidental changes.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Users needed flexibility, but free-form editing could alter key totals and references | Formula-driven invoice sheets with validation, named fields and protected calculation areas | Editable inputs and controlled outputs were separated inside the same familiar workbook |

## The real constraint

Lock the whole file and the worker cannot complete the invoice. Leave every cell open and a small edit can change a total, invoice number or rate calculation without being obvious.

The solution needed a clear boundary between information the user should supply and logic the workbook should control.

## What Heutrix delivered

The workbook used formula cells, validated inputs and reusable named fields for items such as the pay cycle, invoice number, contractor details, claimed hours, reimbursements and totals. The process design also called out:

- protected template and rate areas;
- protected total cells;
- hidden invoice-number references;
- formula-driven weekend-rate calculations;
- guidance on editable and non-editable fields; and
- a final workbook-protection step before release.

The inspected master files contain multiple protected sheets, data-validation rules and formula-heavy invoice tabs. The controls were embedded in the tool staff already used rather than requiring a separate application for every entry.

## The operating result

Workers retained a practical way to enter their invoice information. Accounts retained a more consistent structure for totals and reference fields. The workbook made the intended editing boundary visible and technically enforceable in the areas that had been configured.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 6 control mechanisms covering protected areas, totals, references, rate formulas, user guidance and final workbook protection.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 10–20 minutes less manual checking and formula correction per invoice on the standard path.

The efficiency range is an estimate based on the calculations and validation steps moved into the controlled workbook. Client feedback also supports high data integrity within the configured fields and controls.

## Evidence and limits

Two master workbooks and the source process map verify the formula, validation and sheet-protection design. Client feedback supports high data integrity in the configured workflow. This does not independently verify every rate, prevent all user error or establish payroll, tax or award compliance; those decisions require authoritative rules, controlled testing and accountable review.

title: Pay-cycle reminders arrived with the right link and the right next action
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

A generic “invoices are due” email still leaves every worker to find the correct file, remember the process and decide which cells to change. Heutrix designed the reminder as part of the workflow rather than as a separate broadcast.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Submission depended on memory, inbox history and file searching | An end-of-cycle reminder linked each worker to their own controlled invoice workbook | The prompt arrived with a specific action and a known place to complete it |

## The real constraint

The recurring problem was not simply that people forgot. The path from reminder to completed invoice contained unnecessary decisions: which template, which pay-cycle tab, which fields, which submission route and what counted as done.

Automating only the email would have preserved that ambiguity.

## What Heutrix delivered

The pay-cycle design connected four components:

1. a configured invoice workbook for each worker;
2. a dedicated cloud link to that workbook;
3. an automated reminder at the end of the pay cycle; and
4. concise guidance on editable and protected fields.

Workers could open the assigned file, complete the relevant pay-cycle sheet and submit it through the defined route. The reminder supported a preconfigured process rather than asking the recipient to reconstruct it.

## The operating result

The workflow reduced the number of decisions between “invoice due” and “invoice ready for accounts”. The link, file and expected action were aligned. Administration gained a repeatable cycle trigger instead of relying entirely on individual follow-up habits.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 4 connected components: configured workbook, worker-specific link, cycle trigger and completion guidance.
- **Indicative operating result:** Approximately 60% fewer out-of-cycle payment events, reducing the associated correction and follow-up workload.

The approximate reduction is supported by client feedback and reflects the effect of connecting the reminder, worker-specific file and defined submission path.

## Evidence and limits

title: A submitted invoice became a controlled state—not a mutable attachment
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

Email can prove that a file was sent. It does not automatically prove which version was reviewed, whether it changed afterwards or when it should stop being editable.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| “Submitted” lived in an email while the source workbook could continue changing | Status automation, post-submission change notification and locking after payment | Review and edit rights followed the invoice’s operating state |

## The real constraint

The source workbook was useful precisely because it remained editable during preparation. That flexibility became a control problem once accounts began reviewing it.

The workflow needed separate states for preparation, submission, discrepancy correction and payment—not one broad “done” label.

## What Heutrix delivered

The mapped solution introduced state around the file:

- the worker completed the assigned pay-cycle sheet;
- submission triggered a “done” state for the invoice sheet;
- a later edit generated a notification;
- accounts reviewed the submitted version and either progressed it or opened a discrepancy path;
- a worker could regain editing access when correction was required; and
- after payment, the pay-cycle sheet was locked against further edits.

The design treated the workbook as the working record and the workflow state as the control layer around it.

## The operating result

Accounts could distinguish an invoice being prepared from one submitted for review, reopened for correction or closed after payment. Workers had a defined route for legitimate changes. The process made version risk visible instead of relying on someone to notice that a file had changed.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 4 explicit invoice states: preparation, submitted review, discrepancy correction and post-payment closure.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 10–20 minutes less version checking and corrective administration for each invoice requiring follow-up.

The efficiency range is an estimate based on the status checks and version-reconstruction steps replaced by the delivered state model. Client feedback supports that the status and locking controls operated as intended.

## Evidence and limits

The process board records the status, notification, reopening and locking design, and client feedback supports its practical operation. No flow export or operational event log was independently reviewed. The case therefore makes no claim about payment accuracy, fraud prevention, system uptime or a measured error-reduction rate.

title: Invoice discrepancies gained an exception path instead of an email debate
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

An invoice could look complete and still disagree with the hours or kilometres captured in QuickBooks. Finding the mismatch was only half the job; the team also needed a consistent way to investigate, return and resolve it.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Differences were found through manual comparison and resolved through ad hoc contact | A defined discrepancy decision, worker-notification route and reconciliation view | Normal invoices and exceptions could follow different, visible paths |

## The real constraint

A variance is not automatically an error. It may reflect timing, coding, missing data or a legitimate difference that requires context. An automated comparison can surface the exception, but a person still needs to decide what it means and what happens next.

## What Heutrix delivered

The future-state process placed a discrepancy decision between submission and payment:

1. compare submitted invoice hours and kilometres with QuickBooks time records;
2. surface the relevant variance rather than asking accounts to inspect every line equally;
3. if clarification or correction is required, notify the worker and reopen the invoice sheet;
4. retain the normal path for items that pass review; and
5. lock the relevant sheet after payment is processed.

The related Power BI report included dedicated variance fields and views for submitted hours, submitted kilometres and QuickBooks totals. This connected the process decision to a practical investigation surface.

## The operating result

Reconciliation became an exception-led workflow. The system helped accounts find where attention was needed, while the resolution remained a human-owned decision. Workers had a defined correction route instead of an informal request detached from the source file.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** A 5-step exception path from source comparison through correction and post-payment locking.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 1–2 hours less manual comparison and follow-up for each discrepancy investigated.

The efficiency range is supported by client feedback and reflects the search, comparison and clarification steps consolidated into the delivered exception path.

## Evidence and limits

The process map, invoice workbooks and Power BI report definitions directly support the comparison and exception workflow. Client feedback supports savings of up to approximately 2 hours per discrepancy. The range is not an audited time study, and this case does not claim that every variance was resolved correctly, that the sources were complete or that the solution guaranteed payment accuracy.

## Related Heutrix offering

This is a [Heutrix Workflow Transformation ](/services#heutrix-workflow-transformation) case: Heutrix connected source comparison, investigation and correction into an exception-led workflow. Current scopes define authoritative sources, matching logic, tolerance rules, ownership, the correction path and closure evidence before handover.

title: One Power BI report brought invoices and QuickBooks time into the same conversation
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

Accounts had two legitimate views of the same pay cycle: the hours and kilometres a contractor submitted, and the activity recorded in QuickBooks. Reviewing them separately made it difficult to see where the figures agreed and where investigation was needed.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Invoice and time-record totals lived in separate sources | A cloud-connected Power BI reconciliation report with shared filters, comparison fields and variance views | Reviewers could move from the overall cycle to the specific worker, client or measure needing attention |

## The real constraint

A dashboard would have been decorative if the underlying fields were not aligned. Heutrix first established a common model for pay cycle, worker, client, hours, kilometres, invoice amount and variance.

The management question was not “How many charts can we build?” It was “Where do submitted and recorded activity differ, and what should be investigated?”

## What Heutrix delivered

The Power BI report contained dedicated pages for:

- invoices compared with QuickBooks timesheets;
- variances between the two sources;
- invoice totals and superannuation components;
- hours and kilometres by client;
- hours and kilometres by worker; and
- fortnightly hours and kilometre trends.

Cards, slicers, tables and charts supported both a quick cycle-level view and a more detailed investigation. The current report package was connected to a cloud Power BI dataset rather than being only a static local visual.

## The operating result

The report created one review surface around the recurring reconciliation questions. Accounts could filter the same model instead of rebuilding comparisons in separate files. Leadership could see the shape of the cycle without receiving raw operational records by email.

title: A year of fortnightly snapshots made reconciliation repeatable
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

A useful dashboard needs more than good visuals. It needs the same source process to run again at the next pay cycle—and the cycle after that—without quietly changing the shape of the data.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Reconciliation risked becoming a one-off report-building exercise | A pay-period structure with recurring timesheet and payroll snapshots feeding the reporting model | Each fortnight entered the analysis through a repeatable evidence trail |

## The real constraint

Operational reporting often fails between refreshes. A local export is renamed, a period boundary changes, a field moves or the new file is stored somewhere the report cannot find it.

The workflow therefore needed to define not only the dashboard, but also how each pay period was identified, extracted and retained.

## What Heutrix delivered

The reviewed source library contained:

- a pay-period reference extract;
- recurring QuickBooks timesheet snapshots;
- recurring payroll snapshots;
- a user snapshot; and
- a cloud-connected Power BI report using aligned pay-cycle, worker and reconciliation entities.

Twenty-six timesheet snapshots and twenty-six payroll snapshots were present across approximately one operating year. The report model used those recurring inputs to support invoice, hours, kilometre and variance analysis.

## The operating result

The reporting solution had a repeatable source trail rather than only a finished dashboard file. A reviewer could identify the relevant cycle and the associated snapshots. The structure also made it possible to investigate refresh or period issues without starting from an undifferentiated folder of exports.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 52 recurring source snapshots—26 timesheet and 26 payroll files—across approximately one operating year.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 1–2 hours less source preparation and historical reconstruction effort per fortnightly refresh.

The efficiency range is an estimate based on the recurring extraction, naming and period-alignment work standardised by the delivered pipeline. Client feedback confirms that the refresh process operated automatically.

## Evidence and limits

The snapshot directories, file sequence and Power BI package were inspected without copying worker, client or invoice records into this repository. title: Incident reporting captured the facts once, in a consistent structure
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

An incident narrative can be detailed and still leave the next person without the information needed to act. Heutrix turned incident capture into a structured workflow rather than a free-form account passed between inboxes.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Important facts and follow-up details could be scattered through a narrative | A structured incident form covering facts, immediate response, assessment, reporting, investigation and actions | The record collected the information needed by later workflow stages in one consistent sequence |

## The real constraint

The form had to serve several moments at once: immediate fact capture, risk response, internal review, any authorised external-reporting decision, investigation and corrective action. If those stages were collapsed into one text box, critical follow-up could become difficult to see.

## What Heutrix delivered

The reviewed form separated the workflow into clear sections for:

- the people involved, affected and witnessing the event;
- date, time, place and incident description;
- immediate actions and risk controls;
- family, carer, police or medical contact where relevant;
- the organisation’s reportability decision and recorded reporting dates;
- investigation, findings and contributing factors;
- preventive and corrective actions; and
- consultation, feedback and continuous-improvement follow-up.

A later digital incident database used structured fields for incident type, severity, description, actions taken, witnesses, consent confirmation and submission metadata.

## The operating result

title: Corrective actions kept an owner, a due date and a closure trail
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

The most important work often begins after an incident form is submitted. Actions must be assigned, completed, checked and connected back to the findings that created them.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Follow-up could disappear into meeting notes or broad recommendations | A corrective-action section with responsibility, completion dates, remedial action and consultation records | Each agreed response had a place in the incident record and a visible route to closure |

## The real constraint

“Review the process” is not an operational action. It does not identify who owns the work, what completion means, when it is due or who confirms that the response addressed the finding.

The workflow needed to preserve the connection between investigation, contributing factors, selected controls and the work that followed.

## What Heutrix delivered

The form also presented a hierarchy-of-controls prompt, encouraging the reviewer to document the selected response rather than leaving the action as an unstructured note.

The incident record extended beyond description into accountable follow-up. Managers had a defined place to record what was decided, who would act and when the action was completed. The structure made an incomplete response easier to see.

- **Operational coverage:** A 7-step path connecting immediate controls, findings, corrective actions, ownership, consultation and closure.

title: Structured shift notes created the input for human-reviewed summaries
body:
> **Anonymised Heutrix case study.** Heutrix delivered this solution for an Australian disability support provider. The organisation is not named, and no identifying source material is included.

Summarisation is only as useful as the notes underneath it. When shift information arrives in inconsistent shapes, an automated summary can make the writing shorter without making the record more dependable.

| Starting point | Heutrix delivery | Operating effect |
|---|---|---|
| Narrative notes and routine observations were difficult to review consistently across shifts | Structured digital note capture paired with a Heutrix-delivered summarisation automation and human review | Repeated observations could be organised into a concise review draft while responsibility stayed with a person |

## The real constraint

The challenge was not simply “use AI to write a summary”. The workflow had to separate factual entries, routine observations, free-text notes and the accountable interpretation of that information. It also had to recognise that shift notes may contain sensitive information that cannot be moved into an unapproved tool.

## What Heutrix delivered

The verified source-capture layer used a digital form and response sheet with fields for shift date and time, behavioural or shift details, routine observations, fluid intake and additional notes. The owner confirms that Heutrix also delivered an automation to summarise notes.

The responsible operating pattern is clear:

1. collect information in a consistent structure;
2. preserve the source notes;
3. generate a summary draft for a defined purpose;
4. require an authorised person to review the draft against the source; and
5. correct, approve or reject the summary before it is relied on.

## The operating result

Structured capture created a more workable input for review and summarisation. The automation could assist with synthesis, but it did not replace the source record or the person accountable for accuracy and escalation.

## Approximate operating impact

- **Operational coverage:** 6 core capture areas spanning shift timing, narrative details, routine observations, fluid intake and additional notes.
- **Indicative efficiency:** Approximately 20–40% less first-pass summary preparation effort while retaining human review.

The efficiency range is an estimate based on the structuring and draft-synthesis steps supported by the delivered workflow. Client feedback supports that the automation operated and assisted the review process.

## Evidence and limits

The digital form-response structure was reviewed without opening or copying completed notes. Client feedback supports that the Heutrix-delivered summarisation automation operated and assisted the review process. Its flow definition, prompt, model, output records, review log and approved data path were not independently reviewed, so the indicative range remains an estimate rather than a verified AI outcome. No sensitive note content, privacy-related detail or clinical, documentation-quality or safety claim may be published.

A current scope would require an approved data class, tool, storage, retention, model boundary, reviewer, failure path and source-comparison test before operational use.
